Values, Types
& Operators

Everything in JavaScript is data. This chapter introduces the smallest pieces of that data — numbers, strings, Booleans and empty values — and the operators that combine them. Here is the chapter distilled, with its original figures and code examples.

00 The source

The chapter at a glance

Chapter 1 opens with a reminder that beneath every program there is only data, endlessly rearranged. Its job is to introduce the atomic elements of JavaScript: simple values and the operators that act on them.

“Below the surface of the machine, the program moves. Without effort, it expands and contracts. In great harmony, electrons scatter and regroup. The forms on the monitor are but ripples on the water. The essence stays invisibly below.”— Master Yuan-Ma, The Book of Programming (the book's epigraph)

01 Bits & values

From bits to values

A bit is any two-valued thing — zero or one, a high or low charge, a shiny or dull spot. Anything discrete can be reduced to a sequence of bits. The number 13, for instance, is 00001101 in binary: its 8, 4 and 1 positions are switched on, and 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.

Working with billions of loose bits would be impossible, so we group them into values. Every value has a type that determines its role: numbers, text, functions, and so on. You create a value simply by naming it — no allocation, no cost to you. When a value is no longer used, its bits are recycled.

Key idea: all values are made of the same bits; their type is what gives them meaning.

02 Numbers

Numbers & arithmetic

JavaScript has a single number type. Each value occupies 64 bits, giving about 18 quintillion possible patterns. One bit stores the sign and some bits store the decimal point, so the largest reliable whole number is around 9 quadrillion. Integers below that are exact; fractions are approximations, like π written with a finite number of digits.

The last line is scientific notation: 2.998 × 108 = 299,800,000.

Arithmetic and precedence

Operators take values and produce new ones. Multiplication and division bind tighter than addition and subtraction; operators of equal precedence run left to right. When in doubt, add parentheses.

These evaluate to 144 and 1,144 respectively — parentheses change the result.

Results: 14 and 0. % shares precedence with * and /.

Three special numbers

Infinity / -Infinity

Positive and negative infinity. Infinity - 1 is still Infinity; infinity-based arithmetic is not mathematically sound.

NaN

“Not a number”, yet still of type number. It appears when a calculation has no meaningful result — e.g. 0 / 0 or Infinity - Infinity.

Results: Infinity, NaN, NaN.

03 Strings

Strings: text as numbers

Strings hold text, enclosed in single quotes, double quotes or backticks — the opening and closing quotes must match. JavaScript models text with the Unicode standard: every character gets a number, and the string is a sequence of those numbers. Because JavaScript uses 16 bits per string element, some characters (many emoji) occupy two positions.

Escaping characters

A backslash gives the next character a special meaning: \n is a newline, \t a tab, and \" a literal quote. Two backslashes collapse into one. Only backtick strings can span physical lines.

Concatenation and template literals

Strings cannot be subtracted, divided or multiplied. The + operator concatenates them. Backtick strings (template literals) can span lines and interpolate expressions written inside ${...}.

Produces the string "concatenate".

Produces "half of 100 is 50". Strings also have methods, explored in Chapter 4.

04 Unary operators

typeof & unary operators

Not all operators are symbols. The word typeof returns a string naming the type of its single operand. Operators taking one value are unary; those taking two (like +) are binary. The minus sign can be either: 10 - 2 is binary, -(10 - 2) is unary negation.

The // → lines are the book's notation for “expected output”.

05 Booleans

Booleans, comparisons & logic

The Boolean type has exactly two values: true and false. Comparisons produce them; logical operators combine them.

Comparison

>, <, >=, <=, == and != compare numbers and strings. Strings are ordered by their Unicode codes, left to right — uppercase letters sort before lowercase ones, which is not quite dictionary order. And NaN is the one value not equal to itself.

Logical operators

&& — and

Binary; true only when both operands are true.

|| — or

Binary; true when at least one operand is true.

! — not

Unary; flips a Boolean value: !true is false.

? : — conditional

The only ternary operator: a ? b : c picks b if a is true, otherwise c.

Precedence, from low to high: ||, then &&, then comparisons, then the rest. This is why 1 + 1 == 2 && 10 * 10 > 50 reads naturally.

06 Empty values

Empty values: null & undefined

These two values both signal the absence of a meaningful value. They are values themselves, but carry no information. Operations that have nothing useful to return often yield undefined simply because they must return something.

The book's advice: the difference between the two is an accident of JavaScript's design and rarely matters. When it does, treat them as largely interchangeable — for example, test against null with == to check whether a value is real (null == undefined is true).

07 Type conversion

Automatic type conversion

JavaScript tries hard to accept odd programs. When an operator meets the “wrong” type, it quietly coerces that value to the type it wants — with results that are often surprising. The + operator tries string concatenation before numeric addition; - converts its operands to numbers. Values that cannot sensibly become numbers (such as "five") become NaN, which then spreads through further arithmetic.

With ==, differing types are converted using a long, confusing rule set — except that null and undefined are equal only to each other. For strict equality without conversions, use === and !==.

Defensive habit: prefer === / !== unless you are certain both sides already have the same type. Remember that 0 == false and "" == false are true, while "" === false is false.

08 Short-circuiting

Short-circuiting & defaults

&& and || convert their left operand to Boolean to decide what to do, but then return an original operand, not necessarily true or false.

  • || returns the left value if it can be true, otherwise the right value — handy for a default. Falsy values are 0, NaN and "" (plus false, null, undefined).
  • ?? is the nullish operator: it uses the right value only when the left is null or undefined, making it preferable when 0 or "" are legitimate values.
  • && works the other way: it returns the left value when that is falsy, otherwise the right value.
  • The right-hand side is evaluated only when needed. In true || X or false && X, X never runs. The conditional operator evaluates only the branch it selects.

09 Summary

Key takeaways

  • The chapter covers four types: numbers, strings, Booleans and empty values (null, undefined). Values are created by writing them literally or by name: 13, true, "abc".
  • Operators combine and transform values: arithmetic + - * / %, concatenation +, comparison == != === !== < > <= >=, and logic && || ??.
  • Unary operators: - (negate), ! (negate logically), typeof (name the type). Ternary ?: picks one of two values based on a third.
  • Mind precedence (use parentheses when unsure), coercion (prefer ===) and short-circuiting (choose ?? over || for defaults when zero or an empty string is valid).
  • As the book puts it: this is enough to use JavaScript as a pocket calculator — the next chapter starts tying expressions into programs.
